notes:
I've drafted verse-by-verse notes below, but there are three gaps you should know about first. I didn't find anything from Catholic or Orthodox writers. I didn't find any traditions clearly disagreeing with each other. And none of the sites I read mentioned prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage. Commentators do disagree, mainly about how far Israel's slaughter can be defended (see the end), but none of the pages I read tie that to a denomination. Verses with nothing listed (36, 38–40) are verses where I found no comment.

**v. 25**
- Guzik: the second defeat shows that even a just cause, pursued while seeking God, can cost a great deal. This shows that even though the tribes of Israel sought the LORD and fought in a just cause, it was still a very difficult struggle. There was a great cost for them to pay in doing what was right. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-20/
- Bridgeway Bible Commentary gives practical reasons Benjamin was winning. They knew the terrain of the country better than the Israelites, and in those hilly regions Israel's larger numbers were of no great advantage. Added to this, the Benjaminites were fighting for the lives of their people and for their homeland, whereas the Israelites shared no such personal interests. Also, the Israelites may have been over-confident with their much larger army https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-28.html

**v. 26**
- Guzik: God allowed two defeats to humble the whole nation. Israel needed to see the sin problem wasn't only Benjamin's. After the first failure, Israel was sorry and wept. But it was only after the second failure that they put their repentance into action by fasting and making a sacrifice for sins. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-20/
- Matthew Henry: in the first two battles Israel had trusted too much to in the former engagements-the goodness of their cause and the superiority of their numbers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jdg/Jdg_020.cfm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB): the defeats made Israel aware of their guilt in not repressing their national idolatries, as well as in too proudly relying on their superior numbers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jdg/Jdg_020.cfm
- Coffman reads "all the people" as not only the armed men, but the whole nation, women and children as well. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-28.html

**v. 27**
- Keil & Delitzsch: Israel went to Bethel rather than Shiloh because Shiloh was too far from the fighting. The phrase "in those days" implies that the ark of the covenant was only temporarily at Bethel, and therefore had been brought thither from the tabernacle at Shiloh during this war. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/judges-20.html
- Constable: This is the only mention of the ark in Judges. The people were not seeking the Lord much at this time. He also allows that only the ark was at Bethel and the tabernacle was still at Shiloh. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/judges-20.html
- Precept Austin: The ark frequently accompanied Israel into battle (cf. Nu 10:35). Since Phinehas the high priest stayed with the ark, it was possible to inquire of the Lord wherever Phinehas happened to be. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary

**v. 28**
- *When this happened.* Barnes calls Phinehas a most important chronological statement, which makes it probable that these events occurred within twenty years of the death of Joshua. Benson and Poole agree that these events happened long before Samson, even though they come after him in the book. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-28.htm
- Ellicott contrasts the two grandsons in chapters 17–21. Aaron's grandson serves as high priest, while Moses' grandson has become a poor wandering Levite serving an idol. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-28.htm
- Coffman cites Boling: given the other signs of an early date, the Phinehas genealogy should be taken at its face value. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/judges-20.html
- *"Served before it."* Poole says "stood" means ministered, because standing is a servant's posture, and that being "before" the ark marks him as high priest. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-28.htm
- Gill (labelled "Baptist · Calvinism" on StudyLight) says this was the priest's posture when inquiring of God by Urim and Thummim. Keil says the same. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-28.htm
- *A humbler question.* Benson calls it a more humble inquiry than either of the former. This time Israel asks whether to stop altogether, leaving the outcome wholly to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-28.htm
- Ellicott: This is the first promise of success. The people needed to be taught that even in a religious war they could by no means rely on their own strength. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-28.htm
- *Why did God send them out to lose?* Chuck Smith openly says he doesn't know. Why would God send them into a battle, say, "Go into battle" in which they are gonna get defeated? I don't know and that confuses me. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-28.html
- *A picture of Christ.* One writer quoted on Precept Austin reads the scene typologically: Phinehas pictures the Lord Jesus as our Great High Priest. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary

**v. 29**
- Guzik: the ambush mirrors Joshua's tactics at Ai, possibly showing Israel had gone back to God's word as part of repenting. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-20/
- Constable: Judges 20:29-36 a give an overview of the battle, and Judges 20:36-48 provide a more detailed explanation. Israel's strategy was similar to what God had specified against Ai (Joshua 8:1-29) and what Abimelech used against Shechem (Judges 9:33-44). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-32.html

**vv. 31–32**
- Henry: Israel's main force pretended to flee, and Benjamin, flushed with earlier success, believed it. Some loss the Israelites sustained in this counterfeit flight, about thirty men being cut off in their rear. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-28.html

**v. 33**
- *Baal-tamar.* Clarke thinks Israel split into three groups: one was at Baal-tamar, a second behind the city in ambush, and the third skirmished with the Benjamites before Gibeah. https://www.studylight.org/bible/lat/nvl/judges/20-33.html
- Pulpit Commentary calls the account singularly obscure and broken, and difficult to follow. Its reading is that the "fleeing" army stopped at Baal-tamar and turned to fight. The site might be Deborah's palm tree. JFB suggests a palm grove where Baal was worshipped. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-33.htm
- *"West of Gibeah."* The Hebrew word (maareh) appears nowhere else in Scripture. Ellicott notes the ancient translations read it as a place name, "west of Gibeah" or "caves." Barnes says that with different vowel marks it becomes the usual word for "a cavern." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-33.htm
- *Modern scholarship.* The Cambridge Bible treats the chapter as two interwoven accounts, which it calls "A" and "B." It calls half of this verse an early addition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-33.htm

**vv. 34–35**
- Constable: The writer carefully recorded that it was the Lord who struck Benjamin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-32.html
- Precept Austin sees God's sovereignty working alongside human responsibility here: the LORD struck Benjamin, and Israel destroyed 25,100. https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary
- Keil: this is God keeping the promise He made in v. 28. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/judges-20.html

**v. 37**
- Poole: the ambush came out to take Gibeah and burn it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-33.htm

**v. 41**
- Ellicott says this verse describes the same rally as v. 33. https://studylight.org/commentaries/ebc/judges-20.html
- Pett: with their city burning behind them and the "beaten" army turning on them, the Benjamites could only panic. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/judges-20.html

**v. 42**
- Henry: the people waiting in the towns joined the pursuit. It is to no purpose to think of out-running divine vengeance. Evil pursues sinners, and it will overtake them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-28.html

**v. 43**
- *Text note.* An ESV footnote says the Hebrew reads at their] resting place here, and the version followed comes from the Septuagint. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/judges-20-acts-24-jeremiah-34-psalms-5-6/

**vv. 44–45**
- *Places.* Constable: Rimmon (pomegranate, Judges 20:45) was farther to the north and east of Bethel. The site of Gidom is still unknown. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-47.html
- Keil: Gidom must lie somewhere between Gibeah and Rimmon. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-48.html

**v. 46**
- *25,000 here vs 25,100 in v. 35.* Barnes, JFB, Poole and Gill all treat 25,000 as a round figure for the 25,100 of v. 35, counting only the third day. The roughly 1,000 still missing from Benjamin's 26,700 (v. 15) probably fell in the first two battles. Barnes adds or from some other cause. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-46.htm
- Kretzmann gives the same explanation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/judges-20.html
- *Modern scholarship.* The Cambridge Bible thinks vv. 45–46 are additions by a later editor, with v. 46's total made by adding up the earlier figures. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-46.htm
- *Ancient copies.* Clarke notes that the Vulgate and Septuagint read 25,000 in v. 15, which is most probably the true reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-20.html

**v. 47**
- *The cave.* Ellicott says "in the rock" can be taken literally, for there are four large caverns in the hill. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-47.htm
- Gill suggests they hid in a cave and sent men out for food once the anger had died down. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/judges/20-47.htm
- Pulpit Commentary describes a cave near Geba that local tradition says holds 600 men. https://biblehub.com/judges/20-47.htm
- *The four months.* They lasted until there was a peace treaty (Jdg 21:13,14). https://www.preceptaustin.org/judges_20_commentary
- Clarke: only these 600 kept the tribe from being wiped out completely. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/judges-20.html
- The Berean Study Bible notes on BibleHub see God sparing a remnant of Benjamin. https://biblehub.com/judges/20-47.htm
- *Catholic Bible.* The Douay-Rheims translation (on BibleHub) words this verse a little differently, saying only 600 of all Benjamin were left. https://biblehub.com/judges/20-47.htm

**v. 48**
- Ellicott: the words mean the absolute extermination of a whole tribe of Israel, MEN, WOMEN, AND CHILDREN, CITIES AND CATTLE, with the exception of 600 fugitives. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-48.html

**Where commentators disagree: was Israel's severity justified?**
- **Guzik** says Benjamin was guilty, but there was no need for the complete slaughter as described here. He quotes G. Campbell Morgan that uninstructed zeal, even for righteousness, oversteps its limits. Earlier, though, he calls Israel's resolve to punish Gibeah a valid and proper fulfillment of God's command to Israel Deuteronomy 13:12-18. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/judges-20/
- **Guzik's Q&A** asks whether God or Israel was responsible, and answers "yes": God allowed and directed it, yet the judgment was too severe. https://enduringword.com/is-god-or-man-responsible-qa-for-november-4-2021/
- **Matthew Henry**: It is difficult to justify this severity as it was Israel's act. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/judges-20.html
- **William Kelly** is sharpest. He says Israel's whole approach was purely human. Where was their humiliation and grief before the Lord? https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-46.html
- **Bridgeway** says Israel were sorry that they had acted in such savage haste. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/judges/20-47.html
